Book of Lemmas VI

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Slide the point C along the bottom line and watch the circle that fits between the three arcs.
How to play: Drag C with a mouse or finger, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claim to test how wide the circle is.
Look for the math

The three arcs make a shape the Greeks called an arbelos, or shoemaker's knife. A circle fits in the gap and touches all three arcs. Archimedes asked how its width GH compares with the whole line AB.

Tangency pins down the circle

Let AC = 2r and CB = 2s, so the big semicircle has radius r + s. If the little circle has radius ρ, touching the three arcs means its centre is r + ρ from one small centre, s + ρ from the other, and r + s − ρ from the big centre. Solving those distances gives

ρ = r·s·(r+s) / (r² + r·s + s²)

and puts the centre exactly one diameter, 2ρ, above AB. Finding a circle tangent to three given circles is the classical Apollonius problem. Bogomolny's applet solves it that way, nudging the big circle one pixel so its centre is not in line with the other two; this page uses the exact tangency above. The logic test transcribes the applet's own method and checks that the two circles agree to within 1% of AB over hundreds of positions.

Three lengths in a row

Drop G and H straight down to the baseline at N and P. The proof on the original page shows AN : NP = NP : PB, so the three lengths form a geometric progression. Writing k = AC/CB gives

BP : PN : NA = 1 : k : k²

Because GH is parallel to AB, its width equals NP, and GH/AB = k/(1 + k + k²). Drag C and watch GH and NP stay equal while the three pieces keep this ratio; the logic test confirms all of it at every position.

The 3:2 case

For AC = 3/2·CB we have k = 3/2, so the pieces are in the ratio 4 : 6 : 9 and AB is 19 parts. Hence

GH = NP = 6/19·AB

The article cited below states this exact result, and gives the same general formula as the one above. Archimedes proves it with straight lines through the points of contact; press Show auxiliary lines to see those lines. That article is a page of prose and a still picture rather than a live applet, so the moving picture here follows Bogomolny's BOL6 applet.

Try sliding C almost to A or almost to B: the touching circle shrinks, but GH and NP stay equal.
